gaps.sentence: Only ___ people attended the talk, which was disappointing.
gaps.hint: countable plural; 'only a few' is the natural pattern
gaps.explanation: 'Only a few people' is the standard way to say a small number; 'only few' is not used.

gaps.sentence: There are trees on ___ side of the road.
gaps.hint: singular noun: each of the two sides
gaps.explanation: 'Either side' means each of the two sides; 'both' would need the plural 'sides'.

gaps.sentence: Hardly ___ came to the afternoon lecture.
gaps.explanation: 'Hardly anyone' is already negative — do not add 'no one'.

gaps.sentence: She speaks ___ Spanish and Italian fluently.
gaps.explanation: 'Both ... and ...' links two items affirmatively; 'neither/either' pair with 'nor/or'.

gaps.sentence: There is ___ milk in the fridge — help yourself.
gaps.hint: affirmative statement; the invitation confirms it
gaps.explanation: 'Some milk' fits the affirmative statement and the invitation; 'no milk' would contradict 'help yourself'.

gaps.hint: an unspecified day in the future
gaps.explanation: 'Another day' means some other, unspecified day; 'the other day' refers to the recent past.

gaps.sentence: Every one of the switches ___ been tested twice.
gaps.explanation: 'Every one of' takes a singular verb: has.

gaps.sentence: There was ___ enthusiasm for the proposal, so it was quietly shelved.
gaps.explanation: 'Little' (without 'a') means not enough — which explains shelving the proposal.
